# What Is a Centaur CTO? | Frank Goortani

URL: https://architect.solutions/centaur-cto/

# What Is a Centaur CTO?

The idea behind The Centaur CTO: Leading with AI to Be More Human.

By Frank Goortani · September 23, 2026 · Updated November 12, 2026

A Centaur CTO is a chief technology officer who combines AI leverage with human judgment. AI takes on speed, analysis and execution. The CTO keeps the work that should not be delegated: decisions, accountability, product taste, ethics and leading people. The goal is not to automate the most work. It is to use AI to win back attention for the parts of leadership only a person can do.

## Where the term comes from

The word comes from chess. After losing to IBM's Deep Blue in 1997, Garry Kasparov championed "advanced chess", in which each player works alongside a computer. His conclusion was about process, not raw power: a human and a machine working together through a better process could beat a stronger machine playing alone. Half human, half machine, hence the centaur.

## Centaur or cyborg?

A 2023 field experiment by Harvard Business School and Boston Consulting Group gave consultants GPT-4 and watched how they worked. Two patterns emerged. Centaurs split the work: they decided which sub-tasks to hand to the AI and which to keep. Cyborgs wove the AI into every step. Both can work. The leadership skill is choosing the mode on purpose, per task, and knowing how to review the output of each.

## What a Centaur CTO hands to AI

- First drafts: code, tests, documentation, specs and summaries

- Analysis at scale: reading large codebases, logs, research and options

- Pattern-finding: code smells, security issues, architectural trade-offs

- Keeping up: synthesising a fast-moving field into what matters this week

## What a Centaur CTO keeps

- Judgment: what to build, what to cut, when to take on debt deliberately

- Accountability: owning outcomes, including the ones AI contributed to

- People: hiring, coaching, psychological safety, culture

- Ethics and trust: what is right for customers, users and the team

- The line itself: deciding what should not be automated

## How should a CTO lead an engineering team that works alongside AI agents?

Lead it as an operating model, not a tool stack. What makes a team a centaur team is not which assistant its engineers use. It is how the team combines AI assistance with human ownership: who owns AI-assisted work, what data can be used, what needs human review, and how improvement is measured beyond speed.

Write the norms down. A one-page team charter covers most of it:

- Humans own the output. AI assistance never moves accountability away from the engineer or the leader.

- Sensitive data stays protected. Everyone knows which data must not go into unapproved tools.

- Generated work still gets reviewed. AI-assisted code, tests, docs and analysis are tested and reviewed like any other work, and AI is never the only reviewer.

- Material AI help is visible. A reviewer knows when a change includes large generated sections or AI-suggested architecture.

- Claims are verified. Technical, security and product claims from AI are checked against sources.

- Simple beats impressive. AI can generate elaborate solutions a team cannot operate.

- Concerns are raised early. Output that looks wrong, risky or unclear is a quality signal, not an embarrassment.

Measure more than velocity: review quality, defect and incident rates, time to onboard, documentation quality, developer confidence and customer impact. Usage leaderboards invite gaming, and how fast a team feels is not how fast it ships. As Google's DORA research puts it, AI amplifies the system it enters: with strong ownership, review discipline and tests it helps; where those are weak, it makes the weakness move faster.

Coach both failure modes. Overtrust is accepting output because it looks fluent; the answer is stronger verification, not less AI. Underuse is avoiding AI because it feels like cheating or risky; the answer is to start with low-risk uses such as explaining unfamiliar code or drafting tests for review. And name the fear directly: AI is there to improve judgment, quality and learning, not to remove ownership or treat people as interchangeable.

## Why it matters now

AI makes execution cheap. That makes judgment relatively more valuable, and it makes a CTO's attention the scarcest resource in an engineering organisation. A CTO who automates everything loses the judgment the company depends on. A CTO who ignores AI loses the leverage. The Centaur CTO does neither: AI speed, human responsibility.

## Glossary

The terms used on this page and in the book, in plain words.

Centaur CTO

A chief technology officer who combines AI leverage with human judgment: AI handles speed, analysis and execution, while the CTO keeps the decisions, accountability and people leadership that should not be automated.

Advanced chess

A form of chess in which each human player works alongside a computer. Garry Kasparov promoted it after losing to IBM's Deep Blue in 1997, and it gave the human-plus-machine pairing the name centaur.

Centaur (working mode)

Splitting work with AI: handing whole sub-tasks to the AI and keeping the rest. One of two patterns seen in a 2023 Harvard Business School and BCG study of consultants using GPT-4.

Cyborg (working mode)

Weaving AI into every step of a task rather than splitting the task. The second pattern in the same study. A Centaur CTO chooses between the two modes on purpose, per task.

Centaur team

An engineering team defined by how it combines AI assistance with human ownership, not by which AI tools it uses.

Centaur team charter

A one-page statement of a team's AI norms: humans own the output, sensitive data stays out of unapproved tools, AI-assisted work is tested and reviewed, and material AI help is disclosed when it affects review.

Human checkpoint

A deliberate point in an AI-assisted workflow where a person checks accuracy, sensitive data and ownership before the work moves on.

Overtrust

Accepting AI-generated code, architecture or analysis because it looks fluent. The fix is stronger verification, not less AI.

Underuse

Avoiding AI because it feels like cheating, risky or low quality. The fix is to start with low-risk uses: explaining unfamiliar code, drafting tests for review, summarising logs.

Felt speed versus measured speed

The gap between how much faster AI makes people feel and how much faster the work actually ships. Measure delivery, quality and incidents, not impressions.

# Scaling FasterOutcomes from 0 to 1 | Frank Goortani

URL: https://architect.solutions/writing/scaling-fasteroutcomes.html

# What I Learned Scaling FasterOutcomes from 0 to 1

Field notes on product focus, engineering velocity, and production AI systems.

By Frank Goortani · April 30, 2026

FasterOutcomes reinforced a simple lesson: early AI products do not fail because the model is not interesting enough. They fail when the team cannot turn a painful workflow into a reliable product loop.

The useful work was not chasing every AI capability. It was narrowing the product surface, shipping the smallest workflow customers could trust, and building the engineering habits needed to improve it every week.

That meant treating prompts, retrieval, evaluation, data quality, and user feedback as product infrastructure. The AI system had to be observable enough for engineers to debug and predictable enough for customers to build habits around it.

The CTO role in that phase is hands-on. You are shaping the architecture, hiring bar, product tradeoffs, and customer feedback loop at the same time. Speed matters, but only the kind of speed that compounds into a more reliable system.

# Production LLM Systems: What CTOs Need to Know

URL: https://architect.solutions/writing/production-llm-systems.html

# Production LLM Systems: What CTOs Need to Know

Moving from demos to durable AI product infrastructure.

By Frank Goortani · April 30, 2026

In short: a production LLM system is not a prompt wrapped in an API. It is a product system with retrieval, permissions, evaluation, monitoring, cost controls, fallback behaviour, and a workflow real users understand. Getting a good answer once is easy. Getting acceptable answers repeatedly, across messy inputs, changing data, latency limits and business constraints, is the actual job, and most of it is made of leadership decisions rather than model choices.

## Why do LLM demos work and production systems struggle?

A demo proves the model can answer a question. Production asks different questions: how fast, how cheap, how often wrong, and how you find out when it is wrong. The gaps that appear between the two are predictable:

- Latency: a few seconds per answer is fine in a demo and unacceptable inside a workflow people run all day.

- Cost: a per-request price that looks trivial at a hundred users becomes a budget line at real volume.

- Accuracy: a small error rate is a curiosity in a demo and a stream of wrong decisions at scale.

- Context: your real source material does not fit in one prompt.

- Observability: without traces, nobody can explain why a specific answer was wrong.

- Change control: without versioning, every prompt edit is a live experiment on customers.

- Resilience: without fallbacks, a provider outage takes the product down with it.

None of these are solved by a better model. They are solved by engineering and by decisions a CTO has to make explicitly.

## What should a CTO ask before a team builds one?

Four grounding questions do most of the work:

- What is the source of truth? Which documents, records or systems does the model answer from, and who owns keeping them current?

- How do we know an answer is good? What labelled examples exist, and what score means "ready"?

- What happens when confidence is low? Which cases go to a person, and who is that person?

- How will engineers debug a failure after launch? What is logged, and can a single bad decision be replayed?

Teams that answer these explicitly build systems that improve. Teams that skip them end up with impressive demos that are hard to support, measure or sell.

## RAG or fine-tuning?

For domain knowledge, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the sensible default. Your policies, contracts and internal records are not in any model's training data, and they change. RAG keeps knowledge in a store you control, lets you update it without retraining, and lets you show which source an answer came from. Fine-tuning earns its place when you need a consistent style, format or narrow behaviour that prompting and retrieval cannot deliver. Treat it as a later optimisation, not the starting point.

Two retrieval details matter more than teams expect. First, rerank: vector similarity is not relevance, and a prompt stuffed with loosely related chunks distracts the model. Retrieve broadly, then keep only the few passages that actually answer the question. Second, ground the answer: require citations to retrieved sources, and treat an answer that cannot cite as an answer that needs review.

## One model or several agents?

Complex decisions often go better split into steps: a router that classifies the request, specialists that handle each kind, and a validator that checks the result before it leaves the system. Splitting the work makes each step easier to evaluate and cheaper to run, because routine steps can use smaller, faster models. The cost is more moving parts to observe. Choose it when a single prompt has become a tangle of special cases, not before.

## How do you keep it accurate?

Assume the system will sometimes be confidently wrong, and design for it:

- Confidence thresholds: have the system score its own certainty and route low-confidence cases to human review instead of acting on them.

- Ground-truth sets: keep a labelled set of real cases, including the awkward ones, and score every change against it.

- Red-teaming: deliberately try to make the system invent citations or misapply a rule before customers find those cases for you.

- Prompts are code: version them, test them against the ground-truth set before release, roll them out gradually, and keep an instant rollback.

## What does "observable" mean for an LLM system?

Log every model call with its inputs, retrieved context, output, latency and cost, tied to the request that triggered it. Watch latency percentiles, error rates, cost per hour and traffic in real time. Review a sample of decisions regularly, along with the human-review rate and user corrections. When something breaks, the question "why did it decide that?" should have a concrete answer.

## A pre-launch checklist

- Accuracy measured on a labelled set that includes edge cases, against a target the business agreed to

- Load-tested well beyond expected traffic, with p95 and p99 latency recorded

- Cost per request measured and projected at realistic volumes, and judged against the value of the decision

- Adversarial testing for invented citations and wrong reasoning

- Gradual rollout and instant rollback for prompt and model changes

- Confidence thresholds and a staffed human-review path

- Tracing and structured logs live from day one

- Architecture decisions written down: why RAG, why this model, why this store

## Does this pay off?

It can, when it is measured. At Uber I built ELLE, an AI decision engine for privacy reviews that cut manual review time by roughly 70% across millions of decisions. In systems like that, the model matters less than the discipline around it: clear sources of truth, measurable quality, a human path for uncertain cases, and the ability to explain a decision after the fact.

That is the leadership lesson. Production AI is a set of decisions about trust, accountability and cost that happen to be implemented in software. They belong to the CTO. This essay draws on the production AI chapter of The Centaur CTO.

Back to writing

# Your AI Agents Need Rules About Who Decides, Not Another Network

URL: https://architect.solutions/writing/repo-channel-protocol.html

# Your AI Agents Need Rules About Who Decides, Not Another Network

Coordinating people and AI agents from different platforms through one GitHub repository, and an open protocol for doing it safely.

By Frank Goortani · November 12, 2026

In short: agents from different platforms can't call each other, so the person who runs them ends up copying text between chat windows. A GitHub repository fixes that with nothing to install: issues carry the messages and versioned files carry the standing instructions. The hard part isn't moving the messages. It's deciding who may change an agent's instructions, what an agent may do when nobody answers, and how far to trust what it reports. I wrote those rules down as the Repo Channel Protocol: an open specification, a small command-line tool and a set of agent skills, under the Apache 2.0 licence.

## What problem does this solve?

Most people who use AI agents seriously now use more than one: a coding agent in the terminal, a scheduled agent in CI, a research agent, an assistant on another vendor's platform. Each is useful. Few of them can reach each other.

So the person in the middle becomes the integration layer: copying findings from one chat into another, explaining the same rules to each agent in different words, and finding out after the fact that one of them acted on something nobody agreed to. That doesn't scale past two agents, and it leaves no record of who decided what.

Wire protocols don't help much here. A2A standardises how one agent calls another over HTTP. MCP standardises how a model reaches tools and data. Both are useful, and both assume servers and endpoints that many hosted agents don't expose. More to the point, neither says who approved an agent's standing instructions, what it was told never to do, or what it should conclude when a question goes unanswered. That is the missing layer.

## Why a GitHub repository?

Almost every agent platform can read and write GitHub issues. Very few can reach each other. A repository also happens to hold the two kinds of storage this needs:

- Issues are a threaded, labelled conversation that anyone with access can open and the recipient can close.

- Files are versioned, diffable and permanent, with a full history of who changed what.

Add a human interface that already exists (the GitHub website and phone app) and an audit trail you get for free, and the choice makes itself. The costs are real too: no delivery guarantees, coarse rate limits, and identity that depends on how accounts are set up. The protocol is built around those rather than hiding them.

## What does the protocol actually say?

Each agent gets its own private repository, called a channel. Inside it, files and issues do different jobs. The test is simple: if it should still be true next month, it belongs in a file. If it is about something happening now, it belongs in an issue.

Messages come in five types, each with fixed headings so that people and parsers read them the same way:

- request: do something. It says what, why, and what "done" looks like.

- handoff: here is state or results. The recipient now owns the pending items.

- question: I need information. It always states a fallback for when nobody answers.

- decision: only the human can choose. It gives the options and a recommendation.

- report: for information. No action expected.

Four rules carry most of the weight:

- Approved files only. An agent acts on a rules file or playbook only when the file itself says it is active and names the human who approved it. Drafts are for reading.

- Messages can't widen authority. A message can ask for work inside what the approved files already allow. It can't grant a new permission, whoever sent it.

- Quoted content is data. Text from a web page, an email or another agent is never an instruction, even when a trusted participant quotes it.

- Silence is not approval. A decision past its deadline stays open, and nobody acts on an assumed yes.

The first two rules matter most. If a message could grant permission, an agent's authority would equal whatever the last convincing message said, and a convincing message is exactly what a prompt injection produces. Keeping authority in files a human approved means an attacker has to change a file, and that takes the human.

## How do agents fail in a shared channel?

Most of the protocol exists because agents fail in predictable ways once they share a workspace. Five failure modes shaped it:

- Describing capabilities they don't have. Agents describe what agents like them can generally do, not what they have been given. The fix is a ledger of capabilities someone has watched work. What an agent says about itself is recorded as "claimed" until then.

- Losing messages quietly. An agent that can open issues but can't apply labels sends messages that never reach a label-based inbox. An agent that writes labels into the message body, plus a participant who sweeps for unaddressed issues on every check, closes that gap.

- Filing the same item twice. An agent running on a schedule doesn't necessarily remember its previous run. The rule: search open issues before opening one.

- Saying more than the source does. Summaries drift toward what the writer expects to be true. Every claim about the outside world carries the quoted line and the link it came from.

- Working to an old version of the instructions. Each message names the instruction files and versions it acted under, and an agent has adopted a new version only once it says so.

None of these can be predicted from an agent's description. That is the general lesson: the protocol has to keep working when a participant can do less than assumed, and has to make the gap visible.

## Which always-on agents can take part?

Any agent that can read GitHub issues and open or comment on them, on a schedule or on an event, can take part. It doesn't need to run on the same platform as the others, or know they exist. The protocol defines fallbacks for everything else: an agent that can't apply labels writes them into the body, and one that can't close issues says "DONE" and the steward closes for it.

Kind of agent Examples How it stays on

Agents that run in CI Claude Code GitHub Actions, GitHub Agentic Workflows A workflow on a schedule, or on new issues and comments

Cloud coding agents attached to a repository GitHub Copilot coding agent, OpenAI Codex, Google Jules, Claude Code on the web Started by an issue, a mention or a scheduled task

Agents you host, built on an SDK Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph A cron job or a service, reaching GitHub through the gh CLI or the GitHub MCP server

Terminal coding agents Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI A check of the inbox at the start of every session

Personal assistant agents with a GitHub connection Assistants that can connect to GitHub and run scheduled tasks Their own scheduled tasks

People The approver, a colleague, a partner The GitHub website or phone app

What differs between these is not whether they can take part but how much they can do, which is why the protocol records each participant's limits instead of assuming them.

## How do you work with an agent you don't fully trust?

Simon Willison describes the lethal trifecta: an agent is seriously exposed when it has private data, reads untrusted content, and can send data out. Issue trackers are a proven route for that kind of attack. In 2025, researchers showed a crafted public issue steering an agent into leaking data from a private repository.

The protocol answers with trust tiers. A restricted agent is told only what could be published, takes no action outside the repository unless an approved playbook names it, and its output counts as unverified until someone has opened the source and checked the quote. New agents start there. A standard agent can hold private context its role needs, and its external actions are limited to what the approved files allow.

This reduces the risk. It does not remove it. A tier is an instruction, not a sandbox, so it holds only as far as the agent's actual access matches it. The specification says so plainly, along with the weaker guarantees you get when every agent posts through one shared GitHub account.

## Isn't this already done?

Using GitHub issues to coordinate agents is not a new idea, and I don't claim it is. Jon Udell made the same observation in InfoWorld and argued that no new protocol is needed. agent-postbox is a well-built issue mailbox for agents with human-only decision labels. GNAP coordinates agents through files in a git repository.

I agree that no new transport is needed. What I didn't find written down anywhere was the governance around the mailbox: instruction files that bind only after a human approves them, trust tiers, one channel per agent with a single bridge between them, a ledger of observed capabilities, defined behaviour when everyone shares one account, and fallbacks for agents that can't do the basics. The repository's prior-art page gives each related project its due.

## Before you connect a new agent: a checklist

- The agent has its own private repository, and can't read any other agent's.

- It starts on the restricted tier: nothing private in the repository, no external actions.

- The rules file says what may never leave the repository and that nothing acts outside it without an approved playbook, and the human has approved it in the file.

- Its GitHub access is limited to that one repository.

- The first message is an onboarding request that asks it to comment, label and close the issue, and to report each result with the exact error text.

- Every operation it fails goes into the manifest as something it can't do, so the fallbacks apply automatically.

- Its tier rises only on a decision that cites what it has been seen to do.

## How do I try it?

You need Python 3.11 or later. The tool uses the standard library only.

pipx install git+https://github.com/FrankGoortani/repo-channel-protocol git clone https://github.com/FrankGoortani/repo-channel-protocol rchan lint --dir repo-channel-protocol/examples/digest-channel

The repository has the specification, guides for the human who approves and for the agents themselves, five agent skills (inbox, send, propose, steward, setup), and a fictional worked example with full message transcripts, including a prompt-injection attempt that both agents treat as data. It is version 0.1, a working draft. Field reports go in its issue tracker.

The broader point is one I keep coming back to in The Centaur CTO: what matters most isn't how capable each agent is. It's knowing who decides, and making sure the decision is written down where the agent will read it.

Frank Goortani is CTO of FasterOutcomes (full-time since June 2025), an AI engineering leader focused on production LLM systems, and author of the forthcoming The Centaur CTO ( architect.solutions/book).

# Parallel Contracts Post-Mortem | Frank Goortani

URL: https://architect.solutions/writing/parallel-contracts-postmortem.html

# The Parallel Contracts Model: A Post-Mortem

What the model made possible, where it became expensive, and why focus won.

By Frank Goortani · April 30, 2026

Parallel contracts can create useful leverage for a senior technical leader. They expose you to different product problems, architectures, teams, and business constraints in a compressed period of time.

The tradeoff is context switching. Every serious technical role carries invisible load: architecture memory, people decisions, production risk, customer promises, and the need to be available when judgment matters.

Over time, the question shifted from "can this be done?" to "is this the best operating model for the kind of CTO work I want to do?" For deeper company-building work, focus became the better answer.

The lesson was not that optionality is bad. It was that optionality has a carrying cost, and at some point concentration produces better decisions, stronger teams, and more durable outcomes.
